title: Percent Ionization
short: The share of a weak acid that ionizes grows as the solution is diluted.
trouble: Students think diluting a weak acid lowers its percent ionization.

blocks.html: The weak-acid calculation gives $[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]$. Dividing by the starting concentration tells you what share of the acid molecules ionized, and that share depends on how dilute the solution is.

$\text{percent ionization} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]_\text{eq}}{C} \times 100\%$. When the small-x approximation holds, it is about $\sqrt{K_a/C} \times 100\%$, so diluting a weak acid makes a larger fraction of it ionize (even though $[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]$ goes down).

Ionization makes two particles from one: $\mathrm{HA \rightleftharpoons H^+ + A^-}$ (water left out). Dilute an equilibrium mixture tenfold: the top of $Q = \dfrac{[\mathrm{H^+}][\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}$ falls by $10 \times 10 = 100$ and the bottom by 10, so $Q$ drops to $\tfrac{1}{10}K$. The reaction shifts forward, ionizing more. Algebraically, $x/C \approx \sqrt{K_aC}/C = \sqrt{K_a/C}$: a hundredfold dilution gives ten times the percent ionization.

blocks.cap: Percent ionization of acetic acid against its concentration (exact solution). Trace toward zero: the more dilute the acid, the larger the share that ionizes.

blocks.title: Concentrated and dilute acetic acid
blocks.q: Find the percent ionization of acetic acid ($K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$) at $0.10\ \text{M}$ and at $0.0010\ \text{M}$.
steps: At $0.0010\ \text{M}$ the shortcut gives $\sqrt{1.8 \times 10^{-8}} = 1.34 \times 10^{-4}$: 13%, over the 5% limit. Solve $x^2 + (1.8 \times 10^{-5})x - 1.8 \times 10^{-8} = 0$: $x = 1.25 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{M}$.
blocks.a: 1.3% and 12.5%: a hundredfold dilution raised it almost tenfold.

blocks.title: From percent to Ka
blocks.q: A $0.20\ \text{M}$ weak acid is 0.50% ionized. Find $K_a$.

blocks.title: Dilution and pH
blocks.q: Diluting $0.10\ \text{M}$ acetic acid (pH 2.87) a hundredfold gives $0.0010\ \text{M}$. What is the new pH, and why did it rise by less than 2 units?
steps: A strong acid diluted a hundredfold would rise by exactly 2 pH units. Here the pH rose by only 1.03, because the larger fraction that ionizes makes up part of the loss.

blocks.name: ch-particles
blocks.cap: Acetic acid at 0.10 M: only about one molecule in 75 is ionized at any moment.

blocks.html: Percent ionization is also a quick way to compare acids at the same concentration: a strong acid is 100% ionized, while at $0.10\ \text{M}$ HF is about 8% ionized and acetic acid about 1.3%.

Thinking dilution lowers the percent ionization because the solution is "weaker." $[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]$ does fall, but the fraction ionized rises. Check with $\sqrt{K_a/C}$: smaller $C$ gives a larger fraction.
